citation: Potkonjak, V., Gardner, M., Callaghan, V., Mattila, P., Guetl, C., Petrović, V. M., & Jovanović, K. (2016). Virtual laboratories for education in science, technology, and engineering: A review. Computers & Education, 95, 309–327. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2016.02.002
thesis: STE education lags other fields in remote/e-learning uptake because laboratory exercises resist remote delivery; of the two available fixes (remote-access physical lab vs. fully software-based virtual lab), the virtual-lab route is preferable on cost, scalability, flexibility, and safety grounds. The paper derives four evaluation criteria (interface fidelity, dynamic-behavior equivalence, visualization, collaborative 3D space) from the requirement that a virtual lab must feel authentic, scores roughly nineteen existing virtual-lab systems and six virtual-world platforms against them, and explicitly reserves pedagogy/learning-theory questions for a separate publication.

sections.title: 1. Introduction
sections.summary: Situates virtual labs within distance/e-learning trends in STE; states the technology-focused, non-pedagogy scope; previews section structure.

sections.title: 2. Advantages and drawbacks of virtual laboratories
sections.summary: Advantages: cost savings, flexibility, multiple simultaneous access, reconfigurable parameters, damage resistance/learning-from-mistakes, making the unseen seen. Drawbacks: computational/modeling burden; weakened seriousness/responsibility ('nothing really bad can happen'); eventual need for real equipment.

sections.title: 3. Requirements/criteria
sections.summary: Derives C1 (interface fidelity), C2 (dynamic-behavior equivalence), C3 (visualization), C4 (3D collaborative space) from a single authenticity requirement; excludes haptic feedback as a candidate 5th criterion (unsupported by any reviewed system).

sections.title: 4. State of the art in virtual laboratories
sections.summary: Surveys ~19 systems across five groups (general initiatives, science-physics, process technology, engineering-non-robotic, engineering-robotics), scored against C1-C4 in a summary table; heaviest emphasis on robotics (9 systems).

sections.title: 5. State of the art in virtual worlds
sections.summary: Reviews six virtual-world platforms (Second Life, RealXtend, OpenSimulator, Open Wonderland, Open Cobalt, Unity 3D) as C4 substrates; supplies VR/VE/MUVE/VLE definitions (citing Pan et al. 2006).

sections.title: 6. Trends and future advances
sections.summary: C2 and C4 rarely jointly satisfied; proposes a two-level object-library-plus-shared-space architecture; gestures toward a 'mixed' physically+virtually co-present lab; flags consumer HMDs (Oculus Rift) as an emerging development.

sections.title: 7. Conclusion
sections.summary: Recaps the five-group, twenty-system classification; reaffirms virtual labs as an initial-step complement to (not replacement for) hands-on training under current technology; re-brackets pedagogy as future work.

constructs.label: representational fidelity
constructs.treatment: central organizing construct, operationalized as C1 (interface fidelity) and C3 (visualization)

constructs.label: agency / interactivity
constructs.treatment: operationalized as C2 (dynamic-behavior equivalence), split into operator-training ('lower') and theory-understanding ('higher') levels

constructs.label: social presence / co-presence
constructs.treatment: operationalized as C4 (3D collaborative space); elaborated via avatars/chat across six virtual-world platforms

constructs.label: embodiment / self-representation
constructs.treatment: avatar concept threaded through the §5 platform survey and the Stevens Institute system

constructs.label: immersion (technological)
constructs.treatment: definitional only, via Pan et al. (2006)'s VR definition; HMDs flagged only as a future-trends note, not a reviewed system

constructs.label: learning outcomes: procedural / skills
constructs.treatment: implicit target throughout §4 (robot programming, kinematics/dynamics skill acquisition); no outcome measurement reported

conditions.label: review / meta-analytic aggregate
conditions.design: structured technology survey against a 4-criterion rubric (C1-C4); no primary data, no participants, no measures
conditions.N: n/a — 20 virtual-lab systems + 6 virtual-world platforms surveyed

conditions.label: desktop-3D / non-immersive VR
conditions.design: the technology class nearly all 20 surveyed systems instantiate (screen-rendered 3D, non-HMD)

conditions.label: IVR (HMD)
conditions.design: not a reviewed system; mentioned only as an emerging future development (Oculus Rift) alongside a proposed future 'mixed' co-presence lab

readings.claim: No system in the twenty-system survey satisfies C2 (dynamics) and C4 (collaborative space) simultaneously and well; VCIMLAB is the sole full-marks exception.
Virtual-world platforms remain rarely integrated into virtual laboratories despite offering the richest C4 affordances.
Criterion relevance is application-dependent: operator training privileges C1/kinematics; theory instruction privileges C2/dynamics.
Robotics is the STE sub-field of choice for demonstrating virtual-lab affordances because its multidisciplinary character makes it representative of engineering education broadly.
The proposed future direction is architectural (two-level object-library-plus-shared-space system) and social (a 'mixed' physically/virtually co-present lab), not pedagogical.
Virtual labs are currently best understood as an initial-step complement to, not full replacement for, hands-on training with real equipment, given the current state of the art.

concepts.term: virtual reality (VR) — Pan et al. definition

interlocutors.name: Pan, Cheok, Yang, Zhu & Shi (2006)
interlocutors.role: source of the paper's adopted VR/immersion definition

interlocutors.name: Huang, Rauch & Liaw (2010)
interlocutors.role: cited for constructivist-approach findings on learner attitudes toward VR environments; supports the C4 3D-ambience-as-key-enabler claim

interlocutors.name: Ketelhut (2007)
interlocutors.role: cited pointer for self-efficacy in MUVEs (River City); not analyzed in-text

interlocutors.name: Warburton (2009)
interlocutors.role: source for Second Life's maturity/popularity and barriers to deployment in higher education

interlocutors.name: Dieterle & Clarke (2009)
interlocutors.role: cited pointer for multi-user virtual environments for teaching and learning

tensions.note: The paper explicitly brackets pedagogy as out of scope twice (introduction and conclusion), positioning itself as a technology-only companion to (not a substitute for) Strand B's affordance literature.

tensions.axis: C2 dynamics vs. C4 collaborative space (rarely co-satisfied)
tensions.note: The paper's own central trends-section finding: across the twenty-system sample, systems that achieve rich dynamics modeling tend not to achieve rich collaborative 3D space, and vice versa.

tensions.axis: virtual lab as complement vs. eventual replacement for hands-on training
tensions.note: The authors hedge: 'we may agree with this viewpoint (based on the current state of the art)' while anticipating continued technological progress could narrow or eliminate the gap.
